title: Review: Real numbers
description: Questions on the ideas in this chapter, from one star (a check of the definitions) to four stars (combining several ideas). They come in a random order each time.

questions.question: Why are numbers beyond the rational numbers needed?
options: Some lengths, like the diagonal of a $$1$$ by $$1$$ square, are not fractions
There are only finitely many fractions
questions.explanation: The diagonal $$d$$ of a unit square has $$d^2 = 2$$, and no fraction squares to $$2$$ (:ref{#numbers/sqrt-two}). The real numbers fill such gaps (:ref{#real}).

questions.question: Which statement about $$\frac{1}{3}$$ is true?
options: It is a real number, because every rational number is real
It is irrational, because its decimal goes on forever
It is not a real number, because its decimal never stops
It is real but neither rational nor irrational
questions.explanation: The real numbers are the rational and irrational numbers together (:ref{#real}). An endless decimal that repeats, like $$0.333\ldots$$, is rational.

questions.question: What number does the decimal $$0.999\ldots$$, with $$9$$s forever, stand for?
options: It doesn't stand for any number
A number infinitely close to $$1$$ but not equal to it
questions.explanation: $$0.999\ldots = 1$$ (:ref{#point-nine}). No real number is the largest one below $$1$$: the average of it and $$1$$ would be larger still (:ref{#between}).

questions.question: According to the chapter, which numbers does the decimal $$3.14159\ldots$$ lie between?
options: $$3.14$$ and $$3.15$$, and also $$3.141$$ and $$3.142$$, and so on for every cut-off
It doesn't lie between any two decimals that stop
questions.explanation: An endless decimal names the number lying between each cut-off and that cut-off plus one in the last place, for every number of places (:ref{#no-gaps}).

questions.question: The remainders on division by $$5$$ obey every rule of arithmetic for real numbers. What do they lack?
options: An order: they can't be split into positive and negative numbers in a sensible way
questions.explanation: Each non-zero remainder has an inverse, so all the rules in :ref{#real-rules} hold. But $$1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 0$$ there, which is impossible if $$1$$ is positive (:ref{#one-positive}).

questions.question: Why do results from the Numbers chapter, like $$(-a)(-b) = ab$$, hold for real numbers?
options: Their proofs used only rules of arithmetic that real numbers also obey
Every real number is a fraction
They were checked on many examples
They are taken as extra rules for real numbers
questions.explanation: Those proofs used only the rules for addition and multiplication, which real numbers share (:ref{#real-rules}), so the same proofs work.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the two rules for positive numbers?
options: Every number is positive or negative
If $$a$$ and $$b$$ are positive, so is $$a - b$$
If $$a$$ and $$b$$ are positive, so are $$a + b$$ and $$ab$$
questions.explanation: The rules are that sums and products of positive numbers are positive, and that every number is exactly one of positive, zero, or having a positive opposite (:ref{#positivity}).

questions.question: Is $$0$$ positive, negative, or neither?
questions.explanation: Rule 2 of :ref{#positivity} says exactly one of: $$a$$ positive, $$a = 0$$, $$-a$$ positive. For $$0$$ it is the middle one, so $$0$$ is neither positive nor negative.

questions.question: How does the chapter prove that $$1$$ is positive?
options: It is one of the rules taken as given
If $$-1$$ were positive, then $$(-1)(-1) = 1$$ would be positive too, so both would be, which is impossible
Because $$1 = 1^2$$ and $$1$$ is a whole number
questions.explanation: The proof of :ref{#one-positive} is by contradiction: $$-1$$ positive would make $$(-1)(-1) = 1$$ positive, breaking the rule that exactly one of $$1$$ and $$-1$$ is positive.

questions.question: If $$a = -4$$, what can be said about $$-a$$?
questions.explanation: $$-a$$ means the opposite of $$a$$, here $$4$$, which is positive. A minus sign doesn't make a number negative (:ref{#negative}).

questions.question: Which is true for every real number $$a$$?
questions.explanation: A square is positive unless the number is $$0$$, when it is $$0$$ (:ref{#squares-positive}). So $$a^2 > 0$$ fails for $$a = 0$$.

questions.question: If $$a^2 + b^2 = 0$$, what follows?
options: $$a = b$$, but they could be any number
questions.explanation: If either were non-zero its square would be positive, and the sum would be positive (:ref{#squares-positive}).

questions.question: If $$a$$ is negative, what is the sign of $$\frac{1}{a}$$?
options: It depends on how big $$a$$ is
questions.explanation: $$a \cdot \frac{1}{a} = 1$$ is positive, which needs the two factors to have the same sign (:ref{#inverse-sign}).

questions.question: What does $$a < b$$ mean?
questions.explanation: By :ref{#real-order}, $$a < b$$ means $$b - a$$ is positive. On the number line, $$a$$ is to the left of $$b$$.

questions.question: If $$a < b$$, what can be said about $$-2a$$ and $$-2b$$?
questions.explanation: Multiplying by a negative number reverses an inequality (rule 5 of :ref{#inequality-rules}).

questions.question: If $$a < b$$ and $$c < d$$, which of these always follows?
questions.explanation: Inequalities the same way round can be added (:ref{#combine-inequalities}). Subtracting fails: $$1 < 5$$ and $$0 < 10$$, but $$1 - 0 > 5 - 10$$. Multiplying needs everything non-negative.

questions.question: If $$0 < a < b$$, how do $$\frac{1}{a}$$ and $$\frac{1}{b}$$ compare?
questions.explanation: For positive numbers, reciprocals reverse the order (:ref{#reciprocal-order}): $$2 < 3$$ but $$\frac{1}{3} < \frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.question: When does $$a < b$$ guarantee $$a^2 < b^2$$?
questions.explanation: Powers keep order for non-negative numbers (:ref{#power-order}). Without that, $$-3 < 2$$ but $$9 > 4$$.

questions.question: Cross-multiplying, $$\frac{a}{b} < \frac{c}{d}$$ exactly when $$ad < bc$$. What condition does this need?
questions.explanation: The proof multiplies by $$bd$$, which must be positive to keep the inequality the same way round (:ref{#cross-multiplying-inequality}).

questions.question: Where does $$\frac{2 + 3}{5 + 4} = \frac{5}{9}$$ lie, compared with $$\frac{2}{5}$$ and $$\frac{3}{4}$$?
questions.explanation: The mediant of two fractions with positive denominators always lies between them (:ref{#mediant}), even though it isn't their sum.

questions.question: What does the chapter use to prove $$a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$$?
questions.explanation: Squares are never negative, so $$(a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \ge 0$$ (:ref{#two-squares}).

questions.question: Why is there no smallest positive real number?
options: For any positive $$a$$, the number $$\frac{a}{2}$$ is positive and smaller
Because $$0.000\ldots1$$ is smaller than every positive number
There is one, but it has no decimal
questions.explanation: The average of $$0$$ and $$a$$ lies between them (:ref{#between}), so every positive number has a smaller positive one.

questions.question: What is $$\sqrt{25}$$?
questions.explanation: $$\sqrt{a}$$ means the non-negative number whose square is $$a$$ (:ref{#square-root}). The **equation** $$x^2 = 25$$ has two solutions, $$\pm 5$$.

questions.question: How many real solutions does $$x^2 = 7$$ have?
questions.explanation: A positive number has exactly two square roots, opposites of each other: here $$\pm\sqrt{7}$$ (:ref{#square-root-count}).

questions.question: How many real solutions does $$x^2 = -9$$ have?
questions.explanation: A square is never negative (:ref{#squares-positive}), so no real number squares to $$-9$$.

questions.question: Which fact about square roots does the chapter take as given rather than prove?
options: That every positive number has at least one square root
That a positive number has exactly two square roots
questions.explanation: Existence is assumed (:ref{#square-roots-exist}), as a consequence of the real line having no gaps. That there are exactly two is then proved (:ref{#square-root-count}).

questions.question: Which of these is true for all $$a, b > 0$$?
questions.explanation: Roots split over products and quotients (:ref{#root-product}), but not over sums: $$\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$$, not $$7$$.

questions.question: If $$x^2 = y^2$$, what follows?
questions.explanation: $$x^2 - y^2 = (x - y)(x + y) = 0$$, so one factor is $$0$$ (:ref{#equal-squares}). Only when both are non-negative must $$x = y$$.

questions.question: Which of these must be irrational?
questions.explanation: A rational number plus an irrational one is irrational (:ref{#rational-irrational}). The others are $$6$$, $$3$$ and $$2$$.

questions.question: For $$a, b \ge 0$$, how do $$\frac{a + b}{2}$$ and $$\sqrt{ab}$$ compare?
questions.explanation: This is :ref{#am-gm}, from $$\left(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b}\right)^2 \ge 0$$.

questions.question: A rectangle has area $$49$$. What is the smallest its perimeter can be?
questions.explanation: With sides $$x$$ and $$y$$, AM–GM gives $$x + y \ge 2\sqrt{xy} = 14$$ (:ref{#am-gm}), so the perimeter $$2(x + y)$$ is at least $$28$$, with equality only for the square.

questions.question: What is the conjugate of $$4 - \sqrt{3}$$, and what is their product?
questions.explanation: $$(4 - \sqrt{3})(4 + \sqrt{3}) = 16 - 3 = 13$$, by the difference of two squares (:ref{#numbers/square-formulas}).

questions.question: Why does rationalising a denominator not change the value of a fraction?
options: The top and the bottom are multiplied by the same non-zero number
It does change the value slightly
questions.explanation: Multiplying top and bottom by the same non-zero number gives an equal fraction (:ref{#numbers/cancel-product}).

questions.question: Why is $$a^2 - 2b^2 \neq 0$$ when $$a + b\sqrt{2} \neq 0$$, with $$a$$ and $$b$$ rational?
questions.explanation: If $$b \neq 0$$, $$a^2 = 2b^2$$ would make $$\frac{a}{b}$$ a rational square root of $$2$$. If $$b = 0$$, $$a \neq 0$$. See :ref{#root-two-form}.

questions.question: Squaring both sides of an equation can add false solutions. Why?
options: Values that make the two sides opposites also make their squares equal
questions.explanation: If $$A = -B$$ then $$A^2 = B^2$$ too. Squaring is reversible only when both sides are non-negative (:ref{#squaring-sides}).

questions.question: Squaring $$\sqrt{x + 7} = x + 1$$ gives $$x = 2$$ or $$x = -3$$. Which are solutions of the original equation?
questions.explanation: At $$x = -3$$ the left side is $$\sqrt{4} = 2$$ but the right side is $$-2$$. Every answer found by squaring must be checked (:ref{#squaring-sides}).

questions.question: What is $$|x|$$ when $$x < 0$$?
questions.explanation: For negative $$x$$, $$|x| = -x$$, which is positive (:ref{#absolute-value}).

questions.question: Which is equal to $$\sqrt{x^2}$$ for every real $$x$$?
questions.explanation: $$\sqrt{x^2}$$ is the non-negative number whose square is $$x^2$$, which is $$|x|$$ (:ref{#abs-basics}). For $$x = -3$$ it is $$3$$.

questions.question: What is the distance between $$-4$$ and $$2$$?
questions.explanation: The distance is $$|-4 - 2| = |-6| = 6$$ (:ref{#distance}).

questions.question: When is $$|a + b| = |a| + |b|$$?
questions.explanation: The triangle inequality $$|a + b| \le |a| + |b|$$ is an equality exactly when $$a$$ and $$b$$ don't have opposite signs (:ref{#triangle-inequality}).

questions.question: Solving $$|x - 3| = 2x$$ by cases gives $$x = -3$$ and $$x = 1$$. Why is $$x = -3$$ rejected?
options: The right side $$2x$$ is then negative, and an absolute value can't be
questions.explanation: :ref{#abs-equation} only applies when the right side is not negative. At $$x = -3$$, $$|-3 - 3| = 6$$, not $$-6$$.

questions.question: What does $$|x - 1| = |x + 5|$$ say about $$x$$ on the number line?
options: It is the same distance from $$1$$ as from $$-5$$, so it is $$-2$$
questions.explanation: $$|x - 1|$$ and $$|x - (-5)|$$ are distances (:ref{#distance}), so $$x$$ is halfway between $$1$$ and $$-5$$.

questions.question: How many real solutions does $$x^3 = -8$$ have?
questions.explanation: For odd $$n$$, $$x^n = a$$ has exactly one real solution for every $$a$$ (:ref{#power-equation}).

questions.question: How many real solutions does $$x^4 = 81$$ have?
questions.explanation: For even $$n$$ and $$a > 0$$, $$x^n = a$$ has two solutions $$\pm\sqrt[n]{a}$$ (:ref{#power-equation}).

questions.question: What is $$8^{2/3}$$?
options: $$512^{1/2}$$ only, which isn't a whole number
questions.explanation: $$8^{2/3} = \left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^2 = 2^2 = 4$$ (:ref{#rational-power}).

questions.question: What does $$a^{1/n}$$ mean, for $$a > 0$$?
questions.explanation: $$a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}$$ (:ref{#nth-root}). It is $$a^{-n}$$ that equals $$\frac{1}{a^n}$$.

questions.question: Why must the chapter check that $$a^{2/3}$$ and $$a^{4/6}$$ agree?
options: The same fraction can be written in many ways, and the definition uses its top and bottom
questions.explanation: $$a^{m/n}$$ is defined using $$m$$ and $$n$$, so different ways of writing the same fraction must give the same value (:ref{#rational-power-well-defined}).

questions.question: Why are fractional powers only defined for positive bases?
options: Powers of negative numbers are always positive
Negative numbers have no roots at all
For a negative base, the value would depend on how the exponent is written
questions.explanation: For example, $$\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2$$, but $$\frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{6}$$ and $$\sqrt[6]{(-8)^2} = 2$$, so $$(-8)^{1/3}$$ would have two values. That is why :ref{#rational-power} needs a positive base.

questions.question: Which is $$x^{1/2} \cdot x^{1/3}$$, for $$x > 0$$?
questions.explanation: Exponents add: $$\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{6}$$ (:ref{#rational-power-laws}).

questions.question: Which numbers make up the interval $$[-1, 4)$$?
questions.explanation: A square bracket includes the endpoint and a round one leaves it out (:ref{#interval}).

questions.question: Why is $$[5, \infty]$$ wrong as a way to write the numbers $$x \ge 5$$?
options: $$\infty$$ is not a number, so it can't be included as an endpoint
questions.explanation: The symbol $$\infty$$ only says the interval goes on forever, so that end always takes a round bracket: $$[5, \infty)$$ (:ref{#interval}).

questions.question: Why is multiplying both sides of $$\frac{3x - 1}{x + 2} \ge 2$$ by $$x + 2$$ unsafe?
options: It could make the inequality an equation
Its sign depends on $$x$$, and a negative multiplier reverses the inequality
questions.explanation: Only multiplying by a number of known sign is a safe step (:ref{#inequality-steps}). A sign table avoids the problem.

questions.question: What are the solutions of $$(x - 1)(x + 4) < 0$$?
questions.explanation: A product is negative exactly when the factors have opposite signs (:ref{#product-sign}), which happens between $$-4$$ and $$1$$.

questions.question: What are the solutions of $$x^2 < 9$$?
questions.explanation: For $$c > 0$$, $$x^2 < c$$ exactly when $$-\sqrt{c} < x < \sqrt{c}$$ (:ref{#square-inequality}). $$x = -10$$ satisfies $$x < 3$$ but not $$x^2 < 9$$.

questions.question: What are the solutions of $$|x - 5| < 2$$?
questions.explanation: The numbers within $$2$$ of $$5$$ (:ref{#abs-inequality}).
